lead: UDP is the smallest transport protocol that still does the transport layer's one essential job: it adds port numbers so the receiving host can hand a packet to the right process. It opens no connection, keeps no state, retransmits nothing and slows down for nobody. For file transfer that is a bad deal. For a DNS lookup, a DHCP request, an SNMP poll or a live voice packet it is exactly right: one short question, one short answer, and a retry costs less than a delay.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.1 for ports and demultiplexing, and the IPv4 header and MTU from Unit 4.

blocks.text: A UDP datagram is an 8-byte header followed by the application's data. There is no options field, no padding and no variable part.

Source port (16 bits) identifies the sending process. A host that expects no reply may put zero here, but the receiver copies this value into the destination port of its reply, so it is normally filled.
Destination port (16 bits) selects the receiving process. This field together with the destination IP address is what demultiplexes the datagram, as Chapter 5.1 explains.
Length (16 bits) counts the header and the data together. The smallest legal value is 8 and the largest is 65535, so the data can be at most 65535 − 8 = 65527 bytes.
max UDP data = 2¹⁶ − 1 − 8 = 65527 bytes
blocks.where: 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65535 is the largest value a 16-bit field can hold, and 8 is the fixed header size in bytes.

blocks.text: That is the field's limit. Over IPv4 the IP total length caps the whole datagram at 65535 bytes, so with a 20-byte IP header the largest payload an application can really send is 65535 − 20 − 8 = 65507 bytes.
Checksum (16 bits) covers a pseudo-header, the header and the data. It is optional in IPv4 and mandatory in IPv6.
Connectionless. There is no handshake, no state at either end and no teardown. Each datagram is independent, and the first one to arrive may be the only one.

Unreliable. UDP does not acknowledge, retransmit, reorder or detect duplicates. A lost or corrupted datagram is dropped silently and the sender is never told. An application that cares supplies its own timer and retry.

Message-oriented. One send produces one datagram, and one receive returns exactly that datagram with its boundaries intact. TCP hands the application a byte stream instead, where two writes may come back as one read (Chapter 5.3).

No flow control, no congestion control. UDP sends as fast as the application asks. A slow receiver's buffer can overflow and a busy network can be pushed further into loss, and UDP will not slow down.

The checksum protects more than the datagram. Before summing, the sender builds a 12-byte pseudo-header from IP fields: source IP address (4 bytes), destination IP address (4 bytes), a zero byte, the protocol number 17 (1 byte) and the UDP length (2 bytes). It is never transmitted; it exists only for the arithmetic.

The sender adds, in 16-bit one's complement arithmetic, the pseudo-header, the 8-byte UDP header with the checksum field set to zero, and the data. The one's complement of that sum is written into the checksum field.
The receiver runs the same sum over what arrived plus its own pseudo-header. A result of all ones means accept; anything else means discard silently.
The pseudo-header catches a datagram delivered to the wrong host or the wrong upper-layer protocol, because the addresses would no longer match. It also catches a wrong length.

In IPv4 a checksum field of all zeros means not computed and the receiver skips verification. IPv6 allows no such escape: the checksum is mandatory there, because IPv6 dropped its own header checksum.

sections.h3: Where UDP is the right choice

blocks.text: Query-response protocols whose whole exchange fits one datagram: DNS, DHCP, SNMP and RIP.

DHCP is the cleanest example. The client has no IP address yet, so it sends from 0.0.0.0 to the broadcast address. A connectionless protocol needs no reachable server and no handshake; TCP could not start here.
TFTP carries small file transfers over UDP and adds its own stop-and-wait acknowledgements in the application.
Real-time voice and video: a late packet is worse than a lost one, so a retransmission would only add delay.
Multicast and broadcast: UDP is the transport such traffic uses, because TCP needs exactly two endpoints and a handshake.

figure.caption: The worked example's 40-byte DNS query: the length field reads 48 because it counts the 8-byte header as well as the data, and the destination port is what hands the datagram to the right process on the receiving host.

spec.title: DNS query in a UDP datagram
spec.aria: A UDP datagram drawn top to bottom: source port of 2 bytes, destination port of 2 bytes, length field holding 48 because it counts the 8-byte header plus the 40 bytes of data, checksum of 2 bytes, then the 40 bytes of DNS query data.

examples.question: A DNS query carries 40 bytes of application data inside a UDP datagram. (a) What value goes into the UDP length field? (b) The datagram then leaves on an Ethernet link whose MTU is 1500 bytes, and the IPv4 header is 20 bytes. What is the largest UDP payload that fits in one frame without IP fragmentation?
steps: The length field counts the 8-byte header plus the data: length = 8 + 40 = 48 bytes.
The MTU is the largest IP datagram the frame can carry: at most 1500 bytes.
Subtract the 20-byte IPv4 header. Space left for the UDP datagram = 1500 − 20 = 1480 bytes.
That 1480 bytes includes UDP's own 8-byte header, so payload = 1480 − 8 = 1472 bytes.
examples.answer: (a) length = 48 bytes; (b) the largest UDP payload is 1472 bytes.
examples.check:
data = 40
print(8 + data)
mtu = 1500
ip_header = 20
udp_space = mtu - ip_header
print(udp_space)
print(udp_space - 8)

traps: Length counts header plus data. A 40-byte DNS query gives a length of 48, not 40, because the field describes the whole datagram.
The pseudo-header is never on the wire, yet it must be added when computing or checking the checksum. Leaving it out makes every sum wrong.
A zero checksum is an IPv4-only escape. In IPv6 the checksum is always required, and a zero field is an error.
UDP does not fragment or reassemble; IP does. A 3000-byte write on a 1500-byte-MTU link becomes fragments, and one lost fragment loses the whole datagram.
UDP keeps message boundaries and TCP does not. A question saying the sender wrote 100 bytes twice and the receiver read 200 bytes once is describing a byte stream, not UDP.

quiz.q: How many bytes long is a UDP header, and which four fields does it contain?
quiz.a: 8 bytes: source port (16 bits), destination port (16 bits), length (16 bits) and checksum (16 bits).

quiz.q: IP already carries a total length field. Why does UDP need its own length field?
quiz.a: IP's total length counts the whole IP datagram, header included, and after reassembly spans every fragment, so it does not by itself give the size of one UDP datagram. UDP's own length marks where the application data ends and is the value that must be copied into the pseudo-header. In IPv4 the field is technically redundant (IP total length minus IP header length gives the same number), but it is kept so the receiver can check the datagram's size directly and so the checksum covers the length.

quiz.q: An application hands 300 bytes to UDP. IP adds a 20-byte header, and Ethernet adds a 14-byte header and a 4-byte trailer. Give the UDP length value, the IP total length, and the size of the frame on the wire.
quiz.a: UDP length = 300 + 8 = 308 bytes. IP total length = 308 + 20 = 328 bytes. Frame = 328 + 14 + 4 = 346 bytes.

quiz.q: A sender sets the UDP checksum field to 0000 in a datagram carried over IPv4. What does the receiver do, and what risk follows? Would this be legal in IPv6?
quiz.a: In IPv4 a zero field means no checksum was computed, so the receiver skips verification and delivers the datagram. Corrupted data, or even corrupted port numbers sending the datagram to the wrong process, then reach the application unnoticed. In IPv6 the checksum is mandatory, so such a datagram is invalid and dropped.

quiz.q: Why is UDP a better fit than TCP for a DHCP client?
quiz.a: The client has no IP address yet, so it sends from 0.0.0.0 to the broadcast address. UDP needs no connection state, no reachable server address and no handshake, so a broadcast request and a broadcast reply work. TCP would need a known peer and a completed handshake before any data.

quiz.q: An application calls send() with 70000 bytes on a UDP socket. Describe the outcome. If the application instead splits the data into 1000-byte datagrams sent over a link with a 1500-byte MTU, what does IP do to them?
quiz.a: 70000 exceeds both the 65527-byte field limit and the 65507-byte IPv4 limit, so the call fails with an error and nothing is sent. Split into 1000-byte pieces, each becomes a 1008-byte UDP datagram and a 1028-byte IP datagram, under the 1500-byte MTU, so no fragmentation happens. Each datagram arrives or is lost independently.

quiz.q: Name two services UDP does not provide.
quiz.a: Any two of: connection setup, reliability (acknowledgement and retransmission), ordering, duplicate detection, flow control, congestion control.

beyond: Not for the exam. QUIC, the transport behind HTTP/3, is built on UDP: it adds reliability, ordered streams and congestion control in user space, so browsers and servers can improve without waiting for the operating system's TCP to change. UDP-Lite carries a partial checksum, letting a voice codec accept a few corrupted bits instead of losing the whole packet. DTLS adds TLS-style security to datagram traffic. Search for QUIC, UDP-Lite, DTLS and head-of-line blocking to see why the datagram model came back into fashion.
